# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

founder.order_why: The sequence from context to problem beliefs to current workarounds to interviews makes sense, but screens 15 and 16 are labelled "Interviews · Sent" while I am still choosing how people answer and who gets a link, so that step reads as already done.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 have the same question, "Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies," split by the recency screen. Screens 8 and 9 look similar but are not a repeat, because one asks how many people and the other how often.
founder.missing: Nothing asks whether respondents speak and lipread or sign only, which matters because a Deaf ASL signer who doesn't speak gets only one direction from captions and could blur my numbers. Nothing in this flow asks about the product either: captions on glasses paired to an online phone, the $599 starting price with an optional $20/month Pro plan, or the wearer paying with HSA/FSA eligibility. I also wasn't asked what share of people already use free phone captions and what they spend today, beyond the open question on how they cope.

PRIMARY.order_why: It moves sensibly from whether I talk with hearing people, to whether and how often I lost track, to what I'd want made easier, and then to my last conversation.
PRIMARY.missing: It never asked what made me lose track, like background noise, fast talking, or people talking over each other, or what I did to cope, such as lipreading, an interpreter, captions, or asking people to repeat themselves.

screens.why2: "What should we call this project?" is plain on first reading for me as a founder.
screens.why3: I know what my own company and product are called, so I can answer at once.
screens.why4: The screen is a box to type in, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The name I typed is held exactly as I wrote it, and I am the only reader, so nothing leaks to a respondent.

screens.why1: Right after naming the project, asking where I sell first is an obvious early step, because it sets who I study and nothing before it asked this.
screens.why2: "Where will you sell this first?" is how I would say it myself and I can answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my first market is the US, since my testimonials and HSA/FSA eligibility are all US.
screens.why4: A country value with an optional region lets me enter exactly "US" and leave the region blank, with nothing odd or missing.
screens.why5: It holds US with no region, exactly what I entered, and the kicker still describes AirCaps correctly as live captions on glasses for face-to-face conversation.

screens.why1: Right after naming the project and choosing the US, it is obvious why Keel pins down who this is for and when the problem happens before testing anything.
screens.why2: Deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, hearing people, too fast or too noisy to follow: these are the words I use, and I can check the summary on first reading.

screens.why4: The value boxes hold my answers correctly, but the actor and segment boxes overlap because both say deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, with only the US and weekly-contact limits added by the second.

screens.why2: "Episode" and "count" are research words, not how I talk about my users' conversations, so I need a second read to see it means how recently the hard conversation happened.
screens.why3: I know these conversations happen most weeks at meals, work and with family, so I can pick a recent window from what I know of my users.
screens.why4: The picked 7-day chip fits a weekly rhythm, and count plus unit let me set another window if I wanted one.

screens.why3: I know this moment closely from my co-founder and our users, but a count for all such adults in one 7-day window is an informed guess, not something I have measured.
screens.why4: The five bands cover the whole range without overlap and read naturally, my 8-or-more belief has a clear place, and a belief question needs no escape chip.

screens.why1: Right after asking how many people have this, asking how often it happens to a typical one is the obvious next belief to pin down, and it is not a repeat.

screens.why_b3: The question's words, losing track of a group conversation with hearing people, are recognisably my problem, but the 8-in-10 prevalence line isn't among the beliefs I recall checking, and "had this" is vaguer than my wording.
screens.why_b4: The card stops at the count and never says what this means for the idea, such as that the problem is common but the stage page says it comes less often than I think, so I have no next step.
screens.why_b5: It claims only "these" adults and keeps 7 of 7 and each name visible, but it never says seven people is a small group, so "Holding up" against a bar stated in tens reads a little firmer than the data can carry.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only 7 people answered: all 7 lost track of a group conversation with hearing people in the last 7 days, so the problem is common among them; how often it happens is the open question, so test that next before building on daily use.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits directly above the deciding numbers, 4 at or beyond what I said and 3 short of it, with a median of 4 days out of 7, so I know the answer and why.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7 and my 4-to-7 bar are plain, but the chart never states 7 people (I get that from "3 of 7"), and the legend's "beyond, the good side" needs a second look because nothing can go beyond a range that ends at 7.
screens.why_b3: The Frequency name and the 4-to-7 days belief are the ones I checked, and although "this" is vague, the question right below it names losing track of a group conversation with hearing people.
screens.why_b4: The screen gives the split and the names but never says what it means for the idea, such as whether to narrow to the people who hit this most days or to treat it as a less frequent need.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim beyond those who answered and keeps "3 of 7" visible, but it never says that 7 people is a small sample, so a 4-to-3 split could flip on one answer and the median of 4 sits right on the bottom of my range.
screens.instead: Of 7 people, 4 lost track of a group conversation on 4 or more days last week and 3 on fewer, too few and too close to call, so ask what separates the 4 from the 3 (noisy workplaces, family dinners) and aim first at whoever hits this most days.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly beside "7 of 7 put it in their two", and that count clearly decides my belief.
screens.why_b2: Seven people and the 7 on my bar are plain, but the bars add to 14 without saying each person had two picks, and my 2-in-3 bar is not drawn or stated, only "You said" and my difficulty.
screens.why_b3: The Importance title and belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this result means for AirCaps or what I should do next, such as keeping group conversations as the wedge while Frequency stays unresolved.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible, but "it's the difficulty they'd most like made easier" goes beyond a two-pick count, without saying seven is a small group, and the quoted "which one" question does not match the two picks counted.
screens.instead: Holding up: all 7 people who answered put losing track of group conversations in their two (bar: 2 in 3), and each could pick two, so this doesn't show it ranks first; it's a small group, but keep group conversations as the problem you lead with and settle how often it happens before leaning on it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said today's way falls short", which clears the 2-in-3 bar I checked, though the "for 3" line ahead of it makes me pause over which number decides.
screens.why_b2: The five outcomes and the counts over 7 people read at once, but the bar line stops at "You said their way of following that conversation.", so I have to work out for myself that the bar is 2 in 3 below "Missed a little, caught up quickly".
screens.why_b3: The name Current solution and the belief line are word for word the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The card says nothing about what this means for the glasses or what I should do next, so I have to draw the conclusion myself.
screens.why_b5: The count stays visible and every answer is listed, but nothing says 7 people is a small group, and "Holding up" sits under a belief about "most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults", while "falls short" includes 3 people who caught the gist.
screens.instead: Holding up among the 7 who answered, a small group: 6 of 7 landed below your bar of "Missed a little, caught up quickly" (you needed 2 in 3), 3 of them lost the thread, so keep building on group conversations as the gap the glasses fill.

screens.why_b1: "Current solution held, 6 of 7" gives the verdict and the deciding number together in one line.
screens.why_b3: "Current solution" is the dimension I checked, but my belief that their way of following still falls short is not shown, only the flipped heading "what makes today's way work for them" and a stray scale label, "Missed a little, caught up quickly against".
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what this means for AirCaps, not even whether one person managing from the end seat changes anything, and "When a line fails" tops a line that held.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay honest and the single quote is shown as 1 person, but "a number has no why worth a question" softly overclaims, since Frequency is the one line that split 4 to 3 and whether a why would help is unknown.
screens.why_b6: Though it is only one person, Tomás's end-seat trick adds something I did not type: someone deaf on one side can manage group talk by seating alone, so single-sided loss may be a weaker wedge for the glasses.

The 1 exception is deaf on one side and manages by taking the end seat, so one person suggests, but cannot show, that single-sided hearing loss may be a weaker first buyer; ask about it in follow-up conversations, and note that Frequency split 4 to 3, with no why question asked.

screens.why1: As the first question of a study about talking with hearing people, it is an obvious check that I am someone this applies to.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is the phrase I use every day, and I can answer the question the first time I read or hear it.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I talk with hearing people each week, because it is part of my ordinary life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover every case and do not overlap, and a screener needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of adults who talk with hearing people every week, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two simple options, so it is easy to hear once and answer, provided I can follow the spoken version or read the card.

screens.why1: After asking if I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask if I lost track of a conversation with them this week, and that sets up the story that follows.
screens.why2: "Lose track" is how I would describe it, and I can answer the first time I read it.
screens.why3: This is my life, and I would know whether it happened at a table or a family gathering in the last week.
screens.why4: Yes and No are clear, but No lumps together following fine and not being in a group at all, and the two chips are more than one escape, with "I'd rather not say" not fitting a simple gate.
screens.why5: No product or founder language reaches me, but "group" narrows a face-to-face conversation that is too fast or noisy, so a one-on-one where I got lost would not count, and the next screen's "your last conversation" no longer matches it.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and ends in "Yes or no", so the wording says well, though I would still need the words on screen because I may not catch an AI voice.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes / No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: I just said yes to losing track of a group conversation this week, so asking how many days it happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It is short and plain, and I can answer it straight away with a number of days, though "lose track" could cover anything from one missed sentence to a whole lost conversation.
screens.why3: This is my own week and I know roughly which days I was in a group with hearing people, even if I might be a day out.
screens.why4: One to seven covers every possible answer after my yes on the last screen, the numbers do not overlap, and "I can't recall" fits as the one way out.
screens.why5: It stays on my week and my conversations, and nothing about a product, a company or anyone's labels for people reaches me.
screens.why6: The question says well in one breath, but "I'll read 7 options" followed by seven bare numbers and an escape is a clunky stretch to sit through, and seven is over the five-point limit when a person could just say a number.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on about how many days did you lose track of a group conversation with hearing people? Just say a number from 1 to 7, or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: After being asked how often I lost track in groups, it makes sense to ask which of my everyday struggles with hearing people I would most want eased.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, but the options do not fit the stem cleanly, because 'made easier' does not sit right with 'Losing track of group conversations' or 'Not being worn out by listening', so I have to turn them around in my head.
screens.why3: I live these situations every week and can say straight away which one I would pick.
screens.why4: These are real and separate situations and 'None of these' fits, but the forms are not parallel, mixing things I want to do (following, catching) with problems (losing track, being worn out), and being worn out overlaps with all the others because it comes from them.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company reaches me, and it stays on following and joining conversations with hearing people, in terms I would use myself.
screens.why6: It is short enough to hold when said aloud, but 'Not being worn out by listening' is a clumsy negative after 'made easier', and the mixed phrasing makes the five harder to keep in mind on one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of talking with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Following phone and video calls; Following group conversations; Catching announcements in shops and stations; Coping with tiredness from listening; or Getting a word in at the right moment. Or say None of these.

screens.why1: After asking how often I lose track and what I'd want easier, asking how my last conversation actually went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I understand it straight away, but 'your last conversation' doesn't say with hearing people, and I talk with Deaf friends too, so I'd have to pause and work out which one is meant.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last conversation went, because I live this every day and notice how much I catch.
screens.why4: The options run clearly from following nearly everything to not following at all, 'mostly nodded along' is exactly what I do, and 'I can't recall' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It stays on following a conversation, which is my own experience, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question and five options are about what I can hold, but 'Lost the thread and mostly nodded along' is a bit of a mouthful and the options are long to hear in one go.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed nearly everything; Missed a little, caught up quickly; Caught the gist, missed the details; Lost the thread, mostly nodded along; or Could not follow it at all. Or say I can't recall.
